summary.text: The block at index \(3\) is \((2,4,2,4,2)\), so any occurrence would require six consecutive primes \(q,q+2,q+6,q+8,q+12,q+14\). These offsets cover every residue class modulo \(5\), forcing one prime to equal \(5\); the resulting finite case analysis leaves only \(q=5\), hence only the original occurrence.

full_proof.text:
Let
\[
p_1=2,p_2=3,p_3=5,p_4=7,p_5=11,\ldots
\]
denote the primes in increasing order, and let
\[
a(j)=p_{j+1}-p_j
\]
be the sequence of consecutive prime gaps.

We disprove the conjecture by exhibiting a finite block beginning at an allowed index that occurs only once.

Consider the index \(n=3\) and take \(m=4\), so that the block in question has five terms. The first several primes are
\[
2,3,5,7,11,13,17,19.
\]
Consequently,
\[
(a(3),a(4),a(5),a(6),a(7))
=(7-5,11-7,13-11,17-13,19-17)
=(2,4,2,4,2).
\]
Thus the block beginning at index \(3\) is
\[
(2,4,2,4,2).
\]
We will prove that this block cannot begin at any other index.

Suppose that it begins at some index \(k\). Thus
\[
a(k)=2,\qquad a(k+1)=4,\qquad a(k+2)=2,
\qquad a(k+3)=4,\qquad a(k+4)=2.
\]
Set
\[
q=p_k.
\]
Since the gaps are differences of successive primes, the displayed equalities determine the next five primes after \(q\). Indeed,
\[
\begin{aligned}
p_{k+1}&=p_k+2=q+2,\\
p_{k+2}&=p_{k+1}+4=q+6,\\
p_{k+3}&=p_{k+2}+2=q+8,\\
p_{k+4}&=p_{k+3}+4=q+12,\\
p_{k+5}&=p_{k+4}+2=q+14.
\end{aligned}
\]
Therefore all six integers
\[
q,\quad q+2,\quad q+6,\quad q+8,\quad q+12,\quad q+14
\]
are prime.

Now consider these six integers modulo \(5\). Their offsets from \(q\) have residues
\[
0,2,6,8,12,14\equiv 0,2,1,3,2,4\pmod 5.
\]
In particular, the offsets contain representatives of every residue class modulo \(5\): \(0,1,2,3,4\). Hence, whatever the residue class of \(q\) modulo \(5\), at least one of
\[
q,\ q+2,\ q+6,\ q+8,\ q+12,\ q+14
\]
is divisible by \(5\).

Every number in this list is prime. A prime divisible by the prime \(5\) must itself equal \(5\). We now examine all possibilities for which listed number is divisible by \(5\).

1. If \(5\mid q\), then the primality of \(q\) gives \(q=5\).

2. If \(5\mid q+2\), then the primality of \(q+2\) gives
\[
q+2=5,
\]
so \(q=3\). But then another number in the list is
\[
q+6=9,
\]
which is not prime. This contradicts the fact that \(q+6=p_{k+2}\) is prime. Thus this case is impossible.

3. If \(5\mid q+6\), primality would imply \(q+6=5\), which is impossible because \(q\) is a nonnegative integer—and in fact a prime—so \(q+6\ge 6>5\).

4. Similarly, if \(5\mid q+8\), then primality would imply \(q+8=5\), which is impossible.

5. If \(5\mid q+12\), then primality would imply \(q+12=5\), again impossible.

6. If \(5\mid q+14\), then primality would imply \(q+14=5\), also impossible.

The only remaining possibility is therefore
\[
q=5.
\]
But \(q=p_k\), and \(5\) is the third prime. Since the primes form a strictly increasing sequence, the index of \(5\) is unique. Hence
\[
k=3.
\]

We have proved that any occurrence of the five-term block
\[
(2,4,2,4,2)
\]
must begin at index \(3\). Conversely, the initial calculation shows that it does begin there. Thus its set of starting indices is exactly the singleton
\[
\{3\},
\]
which is finite.

The conjecture asserts that for every \(n>2\) and every \(m\ge 0\), the block
\[
a(n),a(n+1),\ldots,a(n+m)
\]
occurs at infinitely many starting indices. Taking the permitted values \(n=3\) and \(m=4\) gives the block above, but that block occurs only at the single starting index \(3\). Therefore the asserted universal statement is false.
